clinicalPearls: Ischaemic necrosis and sloughing of the renal papillae, fragments of which can pass into the urine and cause colic or obstruction

The classic causes are captured by the mnemonic POSTCARDS: Pyelonephritis, Obstruction, Sickle cell disease, Tuberculosis, Cirrhosis or chronic alcoholism, Analgesics, Renal vein thrombosis, Diabetes mellitus and Systemic vasculitis
Diabetes mellitus and chronic analgesic overuse are among the most frequent contributors, and several insults often coexist in one patient
Presentations include haematuria, loin pain, passage of tissue fragments, recurrent infection or features of obstruction
The renal medulla is especially vulnerable because it operates on a marginal blood and oxygen supply
CT urography, or the older intravenous urogram, shows a ring shadow or clubbed, irregular calyces where a papilla has sloughed
Management is largely supportive: treat infection, relieve obstruction caused by a sloughed papilla, and control the underlying disease
Withdrawing offending analgesics and optimising glycaemic control help to prevent progression
reference.pathophysiology: The renal papilla lies at the tip of the medulla and is perfused by the vasa recta in a region of relatively low oxygen tension, making it highly susceptible to ischaemia. Conditions that reduce medullary blood flow or heighten its metabolic vulnerability, such as diabetic microvascular disease, analgesic-induced vascular injury, sickling of red cells within the hypertonic medulla, infection with oedema and raised intrarenal pressure, and obstruction, cause coagulative necrosis of one or more papillae. The necrotic tissue may calcify in situ or detach and pass down the ureter, where it can obstruct and mimic a calculus.
additionalDifferentials: Urothelial tumour or blood clot presenting as a filling defect
additionalInvestigations: CT urography or intravenous urogram showing ring shadows and calyceal deformity
Urine microscopy and cytology, which may reveal sloughed papillary tissue
Assessment for underlying disease including glucose or HbA1c, sickle screen and analgesic history
Non-contrast CT to distinguish a sloughed papilla from a calculus
redFlags: Sepsis from infection with obstruction by necrotic tissue
Acute kidney injury, especially with bilateral papillary involvement
Rapid deterioration in a solitary functioning kidney
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the number of papillae affected and control of the underlying causes; an isolated event with a single reversible cause may have little lasting impact, whereas recurrent necrosis, as in combined diabetes and analgesic use, can cause progressive chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking a sloughed papilla for a calculus on imaging
Failing to look for multiple coexisting causes, such as diabetes together with analgesics
Overlooking analgesic overuse in the drug history
Missing an infected obstructed system caused by necrotic tissue
